title: Properties of Feedback
intro: A feedback amplifier trades open-loop gain for accuracy, bandwidth, controlled impedances and linearity. All of these follow from one fact: the closed-loop gain hardly depends on the forward amplifier (Razavi, Section 8.1).

blocks.text: Gain desensitization

A common-source stage has a gain $g_m r_O$ that drifts with mobility, oxide thickness, temperature and bias. Wrap it in a capacitive divider: $C_1$ from the input to the gate and $C_2$ from the drain back to the gate. At frequencies where the bias source and $C_2$ load the drain negligibly, writing the charge balance at the gate gives

blocks.text: A capacitor ratio can be held to a fraction of a percent because both capacitors see the same process and temperature. In general, a change $dA$ in the open-loop gain produces

so the higher the loop gain, the more precise the closed-loop gain. There is a built-in trade: raising $\beta$ raises the loop gain but lowers the closed-loop gain $\approx 1/\beta$. One starts with far more gain than needed and spends it on precision. The same desensitization explains every property below: whatever makes $A$ vary (process, frequency, load, signal level) is suppressed by $1 + \beta A$.

The loop gain of the capacitive stage is found by zeroing $V_{in}$, injecting $V_t$ at the gate side of the loop and following it: $C_1$ and $C_2$ divide it to $V_t C_2/(C_1 + C_2)$ at the gate and the transistor amplifies by $-g_{m1} r_{O1}$, so $\beta A = g_{m1} r_{O1} C_2/(C_1 + C_2)$. (Both capacitors have high impedance at low frequency, so the divider still works there.)
The plot shows the closed-loop gain flattening at $1/\beta$ once $A$ is large: in that region a large change in $A$ barely moves the output.
Terminal impedances

Feedback that senses the output voltage tries to hold that voltage regardless of load, so the output behaves like a voltage source: its resistance falls by $1 + \beta A$. Feedback that senses the output current makes the output a better current source: its resistance rises by $1 + \beta A$. At the input, returning a voltage in series with the source means the amplifier input sees only the small error voltage, so less current flows and $R_{in}$ rises; returning a current in parallel diverts input current and lowers $R_{in}$.

Example: a common-gate stage (input at the source, load $R_D$) whose output is divided by $C_1$, $C_2$ and fed to the gate of a current source $M_2$ at the input node. Breaking the loop gives $R_{in,open} = 1/(g_{m1} + g_{mb1})$; with the loop closed, $M_2$ returns extra current proportional to the output, and

Bandwidth
Let the forward amplifier have one pole, $A(s) = A_0/(1 + s/\omega_0)$. Substituting into $A/(1 + \beta A)$:

The low-frequency gain falls by $1 + \beta A_0$ and the pole moves up by the same factor, so the gain-bandwidth product $A_0\omega_0$ is unchanged. The benefit is that one can now buy speed by cascading: to get a gain of 100 from an amplifier whose open-loop gain is 100 and bandwidth 10 MHz, close two copies at a gain of 10 each (100 MHz each) and cascade them. The rise time drops by about ten times, for twice the power.

blocks.caption: A one-pole amplifier with and without feedback: the gain drops by $1 + \beta A_0 = 101$ and the bandwidth grows by the same factor.

blocks.text: Nonlinearity

A nonlinear amplifier is one whose small-signal gain (slope) changes with signal level, say from $A_1$ near the bias point to $A_2 = A_1 - \Delta A$ at the peaks. Open loop, the gain ratio is $1 - \Delta A/A_1$. Closed loop,
so the slope variation, and with it the distortion, shrinks by roughly the loop gain. Chapter 14 treats this in detail.
Noise

Feedback does not lower noise. If the forward amplifier has input-referred noise $V_n$ and the feedback network is noiseless, then $(V_{in} + V_n - \beta V_{out})A = V_{out}$: the noise enters exactly like the signal, so the closed-loop input-referred noise is still $V_n$. A resistive feedback network adds its own noise. When the network senses a node other than the output (for example the source of a transistor whose drain is the output), the input-referred noise can even get worse than open loop.
Four types of amplifier

Inputs and outputs can each be a voltage or a current, giving four amplifier types. A circuit that senses a voltage should have a high input impedance (like a voltmeter); one that senses a current should have a low one (like an ammeter). One that delivers a voltage should have a low output impedance; one that delivers a current, a high one.

items: Voltage amplifier, gain $A_v = V_{out}/V_{in}$ (dimensionless): common-source stage; a source follower after it lowers $R_{out}$.
Transimpedance amplifier, gain $R_0 = V_{out}/I_{in}$ (ohms): common-gate stage taking a current at its source; a 2 k$\Omega$ transimpedance gives 2 V per mA.

Transconductance amplifier, gain $G_m = I_{out}/V_{in}$ (siemens): a transistor converting gate voltage to drain current; a gain stage in front, as in $G_m = -g_{m1}(r_{O1} \parallel R_D)\,g_{m2}$, raises it.
Current amplifier, gain $A_I = I_{out}/I_{in}$: a common-gate device passing its source current to its drain, or a current mirror.

blocks.text: Real versions have finite input and output impedances. Model them so that the ideal case comes out in the limit: a voltage amplifier's $Z_{in}$ in parallel with its input (ideal: infinite), a transimpedance amplifier's $Z_{in}$ in series with its input (ideal: zero).

blocks.title: Gain error
blocks.text: $A = 1000$ and $\beta = 0.1$. Find the closed-loop gain and its error from $1/\beta$. Then find the change in closed-loop gain if $A$ drops by 20% to 800.
solution: $A_{CL} = 1000/(1 + 100) = 9.901$. The ideal is 10, so the error is 1%.
At $A = 800$: $A_{CL} = 800/(1 + 80) = 9.877$. The change is only 0.24%, against 20% in $A$, consistent with the factor $1/(1 + \beta A) \approx 1/100$.
blocks.answer: $A_{CL} = 9.90$ (1% low); a 20% drop in $A$ moves it by only 0.24%.

blocks.title: Capacitive feedback stage
blocks.text: In the capacitive-feedback common-source stage, $g_{m1} r_{O1} = 50$ and $C_1 = 4C_2$. Find the loop gain, the closed-loop gain and its error from the ideal $-C_1/C_2$.
solution: Check: the ideal $-C_1/C_2 = -4$ times $\beta A/(1 + \beta A) = 10/11$ also gives $-3.64$. The error is $1/11 = 9.1\%$.

blocks.title: Bandwidth extension
blocks.text: An amplifier has $A_0 = 1000$ and a pole at 10 kHz. With $\beta = 0.1$, find the closed-loop gain and bandwidth.
solution: The loop gain at DC is 100, so the closed-loop gain is $1000/101 = 9.9$.
The closed-loop pole is $101 \times 10\text{ kHz} = 1.01\text{ MHz}$.
Gain times bandwidth is about 10 MHz, the same as $1000 \times 10\text{ kHz}$.

blocks.title: One stage or two?
blocks.text: An amplifier has $A_0 = 200$ and one pole at 5 MHz. You need a gain of 100. Compare (a) one closed-loop stage with gain 100 and (b) two cascaded closed-loop stages with gain 10 each. Give the $-3$ dB bandwidth of each.
blocks.hint: For $n$ identical real poles at $\omega_p$, the $-3$ dB frequency is $\omega_p\sqrt{2^{1/n} - 1}$.
solution: (a) $200/(1 + 200\beta) = 100$ gives $1 + 200\beta = 2$, so the pole moves to $2 \times 5 = 10$ MHz.
(b) Each stage needs $1 + 200\beta = 20$ ($\beta = 0.095$), so each has its pole at $20 \times 5 = 100$ MHz.
Two identical poles at 100 MHz give a $-3$ dB frequency of $100\text{ MHz} \times \sqrt{\sqrt{2} - 1} = 64$ MHz.
blocks.answer: (a) 10 MHz; (b) about 64 MHz, for twice the power.

blocks.title: Linearization
blocks.text: Over the output swing an amplifier's incremental gain falls from 1000 to 800. It is used with $\beta = 0.1$. Compare the open- and closed-loop gain ratios.
solution: The slope variation fell from 20% to 0.25%, by about the loop gain.

blocks.title: Output resistance
blocks.text: A voltage-sensing amplifier has an open-loop output resistance of 1 k$\Omega$ and a loop gain of 100. What is the closed-loop output resistance?
solution: Voltage sensing divides $R_{out}$ by $1 + \beta A$: $1\text{ k}\Omega/101 = 9.9\;\Omega$.
